newsitem.title: UK: Research finds new link to hormones and mood.
newsitem.headline: Research finds new link to hormones and mood.

text.p: British researchers said on Wednesday they had found more evidence about how the female hormone oestrogen affects mood.
George Fink and Barbara Sumner of Britain's Medical Research Council's Brain Metabolism Unit in Edinburgh said oestrogen helped the brain use more serotonin, a chemical important to mood and sleep.
In a letter to the science journal Nature, they said oestrogen created more receptors in nerve cells for serotonin. The receptors are where a chemical "docks" into a cell.

"An acute surge of oestrogen in the female rat induces a significant increase of (serotonin) receptors in the higher centres of the forebrain, suggesting that this may be a key mechanism in the psychotropic effect of oestrogen," they wrote.
They noted that previous research had shown clear links between oestrogen and mood, but said scientists were not sure how this happened.

"The role of oestrogen in affective disorders (depression and mania) is suggested by the fact that menopausal and postnatal depression are associated with a massive drop in plasma (blood) oestrogen concentrations, and oestrogen has been reported to be effective in treatment of depression in women."
They said their findings provided "compelling evidence that the acute effects of oestrogen on mood and mental state are mediated at least in part by an increase in density of (serotonin) receptors".

Serotonin is a neurotransmitter, a hormone that helps carry messages between nerve cells. Several new antidepressant drugs, such as Prozac, work by interacting with the serotonin transporter, while some hallucinogens interfere with it.
